name: Treadmill desk

lead: A treadmill desk lets you walk slowly while you work. People use it to add low-intensity movement to the day, which supports a leaner physique over time, and some like the upright stance compared with sitting.

Slow walking raises energy expenditure above resting levels while you type or read. Trials report more daily activity and modest weight changes; effects on posture and appearance have not been studied.

paras: Users walk at an easy pace, typically under 2 mph, for part of the workday and alternate with sitting or standing. Weight and fitness changes build over weeks and months.

Studies report slight effects on pointing accuracy and number recall. Cardiometabolic benefit is not established. Safety keys stop the belt if you step off, and some people find fine mouse work harder while walking.

angle.text: Treadmill desks add low-intensity walking to the workday, which raises daily energy use and supports a gradual move toward a leaner physique. Trials show more movement and modest weight changes.

lead: A treadmill desk is a computer desk adapted so the user walks slowly on a treadmill while working. It is intended to reduce sitting time and raise energy expenditure above resting levels, not to deliver aerobic exercise.[1]

Wikipedia credits Nathan Edelson with proposing the idea in the late 1980s, and James Levine of the Mayo Clinic is credited as its popular inspiration.[1] Trials and reviews report increased activity and energy expenditure and modest weight changes, with limited evidence of cardiometabolic benefit.[1][2][3]

paras: Edelson published articles in 1988 and 1989 and received a patent in 1993 for a portable version. Seth Roberts built one in 1996, and Levine popularised the concept. TrekDesk, the first height-adjustable desk made to fit existing treadmills, appeared in 2009.[1]

Three categories exist: desks fitted over a standard treadmill, treadmills fitted under standing desks, and integrated units. Safety features include a clip-on key that stops the belt and automatic pausing when no user is present.[1]

A 1-year prospective trial of 36 employees tested whether treadmill desks would raise daily activity and cut sedentary time.[4] Levine's team reported mean weight loss of 1.4 kg, or 2.3 kg among obese participants, per Wikipedia.[1] A 2021 meta-analysis of 13 studies, as summarised on Wikipedia, found increased energy expenditure and modestly less sitting but lacking evidence of cardiometabolic benefit.[1] Systematic reviews of standing and treadmill desks and of active workstations have assessed health and performance outcomes.[2][3] A randomized controlled trial evaluated a workplace treadmill desk intervention, and a study examined physicians' activity.[5][6] Acute cardiometabolic markers were assessed after reducing prolonged sitting with a treadmill desk.[7]

Studies tested cognitive tasks while walking slowly. One examined Stroop, flanker and reading comprehension in 66 participants.[8] Another study reported that slow walking did not negatively affect executive abilities.[9] A PLOS ONE study of 75 participants reported a modest negative effect on number-sequence recall, and Levine reported lower mouse accuracy, per Wikipedia.[1] A study examined transcriptionists' productivity.[10]

timeline.event: Edelson granted patent for a portable version.[1]
